results.verdict: A largely dignified, agency-forward portrait that honours its dedication and never makes him recant — but a load-bearing fabrication ('thirteen years' / Serpo destination strings invented onto his 2001 hack, even with ch-99's disclaimer) risks welding his real claims to a forum legend he never made, and would wound him if presented as what he 'found'.

findings.quote: Glasgow in the seventies was rain and bus timetables and the public library on a Saturday
findings.problem: Factual error he would correct publicly: McKinnon was born in Glasgow but raised largely in London from childhood. Building his entire formative-years interiority around 1970s Glasgow ('library with the good stamp', Glasgow Library throughout) misstates his biography. The book elsewhere is careful with the record; this is a conspicuous lapse.
findings.fix: Verify and correct his upbringing timeline against the public record. If Scottish identity matters thematically, place it accurately (born Glasgow, raised London) rather than staging childhood scenes in a city he largely didn't grow up in.

findings.problem: The novel stages Gary, ON HIS 2001 SCREEN, deriving 'thirteen years', round-trip-eligibility, crew-of-twelve, and a Serpo-shaped destination lookup. Ch-99 honestly flags this as Invented and confirms these came from the 2005 forum, not his hack. But Movement I 'believes on the page' so totally that a casual reader closes the book believing Gary McKinnon personally pulled Serpo data off a NASA server. That is precisely the 'crank mascot' trap he has spent twenty years resisting. The audit chapter cannot fully undo what 14 immersive chapters assert.
findings.fix: Within Movement I prose itself, do not let Gary derive the Serpo-specific integers/destinations in 2001. Keep his 2001 screen to what he actually described (NTO-style headers, F2F, image) and let the Serpo numbers genuinely first appear in 2005 (ch 20), as ch-99 claims they do. Right now the prose contradicts its own audit by front-loading 'thirteen years' into 2001.

findings.quote: Karen called. Gary sat very still
findings.problem: The book names a partner 'Karen' here and references 'his partner' / 'her nephew' / 'her aunt's home' throughout, and asserts the relationship 'did not survive the decade'. The real case involved a named partner (Janis Sharp is his mother and a public campaigner; the Crouch End household and girlfriend are part of the record but the private emotional interior is not). Inventing first names, phone calls, a breakup, and intimate filter-room-equivalent domestic beats edges into private life he never offered. The 'this book does not claim to know why' hedge is good but the naming still manufactures intimacy.
findings.fix: Cross-check every named living person against the public record (note: Janis is his MOTHER, not partner — ensure no conflation). Anonymise the partner unless her name and the breakup are genuinely on the public record with her consent. Keep ch-99's 'no invented breakup causation' promise honoured in the prose.

findings.quote: Machines did not laugh when you took something literally... Machines, he had discovered early, were the first place he had ever belonged.
findings.problem: The 'machines were where I belonged / social cues are foreign script' framing is handled with more dignity than most, and ch-99 calls the diagnosis 'a lens, not a headline' — genuinely good. But repeated across chapters it slides toward the tidy 'savant who can't read faces' trope. Gary has publicly resisted being reduced to his diagnosis as plot-explanation. The risk is the autism becomes the engine of the hacking rather than one true fact about a whole person.
findings.fix: Trim one or two of the 'machines vs faces' restatements. Let his competence and curiosity stand on their own at least once without routing through the diagnosis as causal explanation.

findings.quote: malice was the only story that travelled well across an ocean
findings.problem: The framing of the US case is sympathetic to Gary (good for him), but flattens the prosecution into pure bad-faith spectacle. He has been careful in interviews not to deny that real systems were accessed; an overly villainised US side can read as special-pleading that undermines his credibility with the very sceptics he wants to persuade.
findings.fix: Allow one beat acknowledging the access genuinely happened and was serious, even as you frame the extradition response as disproportionate — this strengthens, not weakens, his dignity.

findings.problem: The Zulu 'Sawubona' / 'Hamba kahle' register and the South African 'I see you' framing is a beautiful sentiment but culturally unmoored from a Scottish-English systems administrator. It risks a false note — borrowed gravitas that isn't his idiom.
findings.fix: Consider whether this lands or imports an unrelated cultural frame onto him. If kept, footnote the authorial choice as the narrator's voice, not his.

findings.quote: widely reported as **97** computers (exact scope disputed in US/UK filings)
findings.problem: Correctly hedged. Minor: front-matter states '97 systems alleged' as if settled, while ch-99 disputes scope. Ensure consistency so he can't catch the book contradicting itself on his own numbers.
findings.fix: Align front-matter and ch-99 phrasing on the 97 figure (allege/disputed in both).

done_well: The dedication's promise — 'never required to recant' — is genuinely kept: every chapter ends with him still standing, still knowing, never humiliated or 'cured' of his account.

Ch-99 is an honest, load-bearing audit that explicitly bins 'thirteen years' and '4680' as Invented and Zeta Reticuli/Serpo as Legend NOT among his claims — it sides FOR his real record by separating documented access from disputed meaning.

Section IV ('Mundane vs exotic readings') refuses to make him a crank OR a prophet, leaving the sceptic reading available with dignity — this protects him from the conspiracy-mascot trap better than most treatments.
His core identity claim — 'systems administrator', not 'UFO hacker' — is foregrounded and mourned as the truest, least sellable title (Ch 14), which honours how he actually describes himself.
The autism diagnosis is framed as 'a clinic relief and a headline weapon simultaneously' (Ch 12) — a nuanced, non-exploitative rendering of medical vulnerability.
'They never showed his files in court' is treated as his real, repeatable grievance rather than invented melodrama, and the May/CPS timeline is accurately rendered.

The Serpo Movement II is clearly walled off in front matter, ch-99, and Ch 22's explicit '*authorial imagining — not sourced from Gary McKinnon*' tag — the structural boundary intent is sincere, even where the immersive prose strains it.
